title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories

paper.title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
paper.abstract: Abstract Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional ϕ 4 \phi^{4} theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data.

sections.heading: Introduction.
sections.text: Lattice field theory (LFT) is a cornerstone of the study of non-perturbative quantum field theories [ 56 , 17 , 16 , 37 ] . In lattice quantum chromodynamics in particular, first-principles simulations deliver quantities of direct phenomenological relevance such as quark masses, meson decay constants, and the strong coupling constant, all at controlled precision [ 22 , 36 ] . These quantities are obtained from expectation values of observables, evaluated by sampling field configurations according to the Boltzmann distribution defined by the lattice action. The standard framework for this task is Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), most commonly Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) [ 19 ] . However, as one approaches the critical region or continuum limit of the theory, MCMC suffers from critical slowing down [ 57 , 58 , 42 ] due to the long range correlation where the integrated autocorrelation time and the statistical error on some important observable grows at fixed chain length. Producing a fixed number of effectively independent configurations therefore becomes rapidly more expensive precisely in the regimes of physical interest. Generative samplers offer a promising route to mitigating critical slowing down by directly producing statistically independent field configurations [ 34 , 27 , 40 , 6 , 55 , 43 ] . Substantial progress has been made with normalizing flows, from sampling scalar field theories [ 6 , 38 , 13 , 14 , 45 , 44 , 39 , 31 , 20 , 9 , 48 , 24 ] to constructing samplers for lattice gauge theories [ 32 , 2 , 46 , 3 , 8 , 23 , 21 , 47 , 12 ] and developing approaches to address topological freezing [ 32 , 46 , 11 , 49 ] . Despite these advances, the computational cost and architectural requirements of normalizing flows remain important limitations. Coupling-based flows impose architectural constraints to retain tractable density evaluation, while continuous normalizing flows offer greater architectural flexibility at the cost of expensive numerical integration and divergence evaluation during training. Diffusion models provide an alternative to these flow-based approaches. Their success in machine learning applications [ 27 , 50 ] has motivated growing interest in lattice field theory, with applications to scalar field theories [ 55 , 54 , 51 ] and lattice gauge theories [ 60 , 33 , 1 , 35 , 7 , 53 ] . A central obstacle to the practical use of diffusion models in lattice field theory is their reliance on representative training data or computationally expensive annealing procedures. Generating training ensembles with MCMC can reintroduce the original sampling bottleneck, while annealing-based approaches incur additional costs through sampling and correction steps across intermediate distributions. These limitations motivate a simple and computationally efficient data-free training approach that learns directly from the lattice action. Recent work in the machine learning community has introduced data-free approaches to training diffusion samplers, including methods based on reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence over path measures [ 59 , 10 , 52 ] , computationally expensive MCMC guided by the denoising score identity (DSI) [ 28 , 25 ] , and target score matching (TSM) [ 18 ] , which relies on the target density and its gradient. However, their efficient application to lattice field theory remains challenging. For instance, importance-weighted methods, such as iDEM [ 5 ] are sensitive to poor overlap between proposal and target distributions, which can become increasingly severe as the lattice volume grows. Other approaches incur additional computational costs through trajectory-based training, as in SPS [ 15 ] or sampling and correction across intermediate distributions, as in PITA [ 4 ] . In this work, we establish TSM as a practical framework for data-free diffusion sampling in lattice field theory. TSM relates the diffusion score to the target-density gradient, allowing the lattice action to supply the learning signal. The model generates and periodically refreshes its own training configurations, as in iDEM [ 5 ] but learns through an unweighted, self-consistent objective that avoids importance-weight fluctuations during training, To stabilize this learning process, we combine a control-variate score target [ 29 ] , which balances action-gradient and denoising information through a closed-form variance-minimizing coefficient, with a noise schedule normalized to fixed total variance. The resulting training procedure requires neither precomputed target ensembles nor a model-density evaluation. We demonstrate the approach in two-dimensional scalar field theory across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases, obtaining asymptotically unbiased estimates of physical observables through importance reweighting. At criticality, the sampler achieves efficiencies comparable to the corresponding diffusion models trained on HMC ensembles, demonstrating that reference data are not required to achieve this sampling performance. The unweighted training scheme enables stable learning and efficient sampling at lattice volumes where importance-weighted training becomes unstable. These results establish a practical route to learning equilibrium lattice distributions directly from the action, retaining accurate physical predictions while avoiding the costs of generating MCMC training ensembles and performing additional annealing procedures.

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: We have demonstrated that diffusion models can be trained for equilibrium sampling in lattice field theory without requiring reference configurations from the target distribution or a costly annealing procedure. By exploiting the target score identity (TSI), our approach enables data-free training using self-generated configurations. Our benchmarks in two-dimensional ϕ 4 \phi^{4} theory show that blending denoising score identity (DSI) with optimal balance—yielding the control variate score identity (CVSI)—significantly improves sampler performance, and importance weighting—which fixes the expectation of the target score across training steps—is harmful for stability due to its large variance. Our suitable choice of training targets enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Remarkably, the resulting samplers achieve performance comparable to models trained on HMC reference data, demonstrating that access to target-distributed training samples is not a prerequisite for effective diffusion-based sampling. This opens a promising direction for developing generative samplers for lattice field theories where generating reference configurations is itself computationally expensive. Several promising directions remain for future work. Since our data-free training approach is orthogonal to annealing-based methods, combining the two could further improve scalability and enable sampling on larger lattices. Its compatibility with multilevel sampling strategies also warrants investigation. Beyond scalar field theories, extending the approach to lattice gauge theories and larger lattice volumes will be important for establishing its broader applicability.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.18863v1 [hep-lat] 13 Oct 2026 Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories Dennis Grinwald Correspondence: dennis.grinwald@tu-berlin.de Affiliation: Berlin Institute for the Foundations of Learning and Data (BIFOLD), Germany Affiliation: Technische Universität Berlin, Germany Ankur Singha Correspondence: a.singha@tu-berlin.de Affiliation: Berlin Institute for the Foundations of Learning and Data (BIFOLD), Germany Affiliation: Technische Universität Berlin, Germany Khaled Kahouli Affiliation: Berlin Institute for the Foundations of Learning and Data (BIFOLD), Germany Affiliation: Technische Universität Berlin, Germany Karl Jansen Affiliation: Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron (DESY), Platanenallee 6, 15738 Zeuthen, Germany Affiliation: Computation-Based Science and Technology Research Center, The Cyprus Institute, Nicosia, Cyprus Shinichi Nakajima Correspondence: nakajima@tu-berlin.de Affiliation: Berlin Institute for the Foundations of Learning and Data (BIFOLD), Germany Affiliation: Technische Universität Berlin, Germany Affiliation: RIKEN Center for Advanced Intelligence Project (AIP), Japan October 13, 2026 Abstract Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional ϕ 4 \phi^{4} theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data. Introduction. Lattice field theory (LFT) is a cornerstone of the study of non-perturbative quantum field theories [ 56 , 17 , 16 , 37 ] . In lattice quantum chromodynamics in particular, first-principles simulations deliver quantities of direct phenomenological relevance such as quark masses, meson decay constants, and the strong coupling constant, all at controlled precision [ 22 , 36 ] . These quantities are obtained from expectation values of observables, evaluated by sampling field configurations according to the Boltzmann distribution defined by the lattice action. The standard framework for this task is Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), most commonly Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) [ 19 ] . However, as one approaches the critical region or continuum limit of the theory, MCMC suffers from critical slowing down [ 57 , 58 , 42 ] due to the long range correlation where the integrated autocorrelation time and the statistical error on some important observable grows at fixed chain length. Producing a fixed number of effectively independent configurations therefore becomes rapidly more expensive precisely in the regimes of physical interest. Generative samplers offer a promising route to mitigating critical slowing down by directly producing statistically independent field configurations [ 34 , 27 , 40 , 6 , 55 , 43 ] . Substantial progress has been made with normalizing flows, from sampling scalar field theories [ 6 , 38 , 13 , 14 , 45 , 44 , 39 , 31 , 20 , 9 , 48 , 24 ] to constructing samplers for lattice gauge theories [ 32 , 2 , 46 , 3 , 8 , 23 , 21 , 47 , 12 ] and developing approaches to address topological freezing [ 32 , 46 , 11 , 49 ] . Despite these advances, the computational cost and architectural requirements of normalizing flows remain important limitations. Coupling-based flows impose architectural constraints to retain tractable density evaluation, while continuous normalizing flows offer greater architectural flexibility at the cost of expensive numerical integration and divergence evaluation during training. Diffusion models provide an alternative to these flow-based approaches. Their success in machine learning applications [ 27 , 50 ] has motivated growing interest in lattice field theory, with applications to scalar field theories [ 55 , 54 , 51 ] and lattice gauge theories [ 60 , 33 , 1 , 35 , 7 , 53 ] . A central obstacle to the practical use of diffusion models in lattice field theory is their reliance on representative training data or computationally expensive annealing procedures. Generating training ensembles with MCMC can reintroduce the original sampling bottleneck, while annealing-based approaches incur additional costs through sampling and correction steps across intermediate distributions. These limitations motivate a simple and computationally efficient data-free training approach that learns directly from the lattice action. Recent work in the machine learning community has introduced data-free approaches to training diffusion samplers, including methods based on reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence over path measures [ 59 , 10 , 52 ] , computationally expensive MCMC guided by the denoising score identity (DSI) [ 28 , 25 ] , and target score matching (TSM) [ 18 ] , which relies on the target density and its gradient. However, their efficient application to lattice field theory remains challenging. For instance, importance-weighted methods, such as iDEM [ 5 ] are sensitive to poor overlap between proposal and target distributions, which can become increasingly severe as the lattice volume grows. Other approaches incur additional computational costs through trajectory-based training, as in SPS [ 15 ] or sampling and correction across intermediate distributions, as in PITA [ 4 ] . In this work, we establish TSM as a practical framework for data-free diffusion sampling in lattice field theory. TSM relates the diffusion score to the target-density gradient, allowing the lattice action to supply the learning signal. The model generates and periodically refreshes its own training configurations, as in iDEM [ 5 ] but learns through an unweighted, self-consistent objective that avoids importance-weight fluctuations during training, To stabilize this learning process, we combine a control-variate score target [ 29 ] , which balances action-gradient and denoising information through a closed-form variance-minimizing coefficient, with a noise schedule normalized to fixed total variance. The resulting training procedure requires neither precomputed target ensembles nor a model-density evaluation. We demonstrate the approach in two-dimensional scalar field theory across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases, obtaining asymptotically unbiased estimates of physical observables through importance reweighting. At criticality, the sampler achieves efficiencies comparable to the corresponding diffusion models trained on HMC ensembles, demonstrating that reference data are not required to achieve this sampling performance. The unweighted training scheme enables stable learning and efficient sampling at lattice volumes where importance-weighted training becomes unstable. These results establish a practical route to learning equilibrium lattice distributions directly from the action, retaining accurate physical predictions while avoiding the costs of generating MCMC training ensembles and performing additional annealing procedures. Method. These results again highlight the importance of controlling target variance for stable and efficient data-free training. Conclusion. We have demonstrated that diffusion models can be trained for equilibrium sampling in lattice field theory without requiring reference configurations from the target distribution or a costly annealing procedure. By exploiting the target score identity (TSI), our approach enables data-free training using self-generated configurations. Our benchmarks in two-dimensional ϕ 4 \phi^{4} theory show that blending denoising score identity (DSI) with optimal balance—yielding the control variate score identity (CVSI)—significantly improves sampler performance, and importance weighting—which fixes the expectation of the target score across training steps—is harmful for stability due to its large variance. Our suitable choice of training targets enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Remarkably, the resulting samplers achieve performance comparable to models trained on HMC reference data, demonstrating that access to target-distributed training samples is not a prerequisite for effective diffusion-based sampling. This opens a promising direction for developing generative samplers for lattice field theories where generating reference configurations is itself computationally expensive. Several promising directions remain for future work. Since our data-free training approach is orthogonal to annealing-based methods, combining the two could further improve scalability and enable sampling on larger lattices. Its compatibility with multilevel sampling strategies also warrants investigation. Beyond scalar field theories, extending the approach to lattice gauge theories and larger lattice volumes will be important for establishing its broader applicability.
